## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Constraints-Led Return to Performance Resources

Trusted sources for this workspace. Local paths point into Eric's SecondBrain library:
`~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/` (abbreviated `LIB/` below). Those
briefs are already ingested and citable — prefer them over web sources.

## The four practitioners this course is built around

Names verified 2026-09-01. Two were misheard in the original brief; corrected here.

- **Shawn Myszka** — Emergent Movement; movement-skill acquisition with NFL players. Co-author on the anchor football paper below. *(Brief said "Shawn Misca".)*
- **Tyler Yearby** — Emergence; ecological practice design in American football. Lead author on the anchor paper. *(Brief said "Tyler Yerby".)*
- **Rob Gray** — Professor, Arizona State University. Host of the [Perception & Action Podcast](https://perceptionaction.com/). Author of *How We Learn to Move*, *How to Be an Ecological Coach*, and *Learning to Optimize Movement*. The most accessible on-ramp for a clinician.
- **Harjiv Singh, PhD** — Motor learning and control (PhD, UNLV); University of Michigan HPSSC and Sr. Performance & Development Scientist, Charlotte Hornets (previously Orlando Magic). Works the practice-design-in-rehab seam specifically. *(Brief said "Jasmeen Singh"; corrected on the strength of five co-authorships in Eric's own Zotero library, then confirmed against his U-M profile and LinkedIn.)* [U-M profile](https://hpssc.umich.edu/staff-member/harjiv-singh/) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/harjivsingh0919/) · [X](https://x.com/singh_harjiv)
  **Eric is already a 1st-degree LinkedIn connection (525+ mutual connections).** A direct message is available and is probably the highest-leverage thing in this whole file.

## THE TEXTBOOK

- **Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Gray, R.** *Enhancing Skill in American Football: Revolutionizing Practice Design for Transfer to Game Day.* ISBN 9798298178846. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Enhancing-skill-American-football-Revolutionizing/dp/B0FMQWN1NK)
  **Three of the four named practitioners, one book, this exact topic, this exact sport.** Eric owns a paper copy as of 2026-09-01. This should be the spine of the course, ahead of every journal paper below. Ingest via the `ingest-book` skill once scanned — see `NOTES.md` for the scanning route.

  Myszka's other titles (*The Problem-Solving Athlete* series: *Coaching the Problem-Solving Athlete*, *Become One With the Game*, *The Lifelong Athlete*) are adjacent but not football-specific. Skip unless the mission widens.

## Knowledge — Anchor sources (already in the library)

- **Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024).** Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698)
  `LIB/yearby-2024-applying-an-ecological-approach-to-practice-design-in-american-football-some-case-examples.md`
  **The single most on-mission paper in the library.** Translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and the CLA into two concrete American-football cases. Use for: the whole spine of the course; every worked football example.

- **Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Davids, K. (2024).** *Being Water*: How key ideas from the practice of Bruce Lee align with contemporary theorizing in movement skill acquisition. *Sport, Education and Society*. [doi:10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701](https://doi.org/10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701)
  `LIB/mokha-undated-american-football-position-does-not-influence-symmetry-in-joint-power-during-high-speed-ru.md`
  Use for: caution about symmetry metrics as a readiness proxy.

## Knowledge — External, not yet in the library

- **[Perception & Action Podcast](https://perceptionaction.com/) — Rob Gray.** Long back-catalogue; episodes on rehab and the CLA. Use for: Joe's commute listening between lessons.
- **Davids, K., Button, C., & Bennett, S. — *Dynamics of Skill Acquisition: An Ecological Dynamics Approach* (2nd ed.).** [Human Kinetics](https://us.humankinetics.com/products/dynamics-of-skill-acquisition-2nd-edition). The academic root text. Heavier than Gray; reference, not reading.
- **"Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Rehabilitation as a Complex Adaptive Process: From Control–Chaos to Actionable Return-to-Sport Decisions."** [PMC12649574](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12649574/). Directly joins Taberner's control-chaos continuum to ecological dynamics. **Strong candidate to ingest into the library next.**

## Knowledge — Found in Zotero on 2026-09-01 (NOT in the SecondBrain briefs)

The SecondBrain library holds 254 paper briefs. **Zotero holds 3,308 items.** Searching
Zotero directly surfaced a much stronger set. Retrieve any of these with
`zotero-research-library-pp-cli cite <key>` or `items get <key>`.

**Tier 1 — build the course on these:**

- **Teune, B., Singh, H., & Robertson, S. (2026).** Perspectives on sports analytics to inform constraint manipulation, representative learning and functional variability in practice design. *Human Movement Science*. [doi:10.1016/j.humov.2025.103447](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2025.103447) · `key=RGAXPJ5E`
  **This is effectively the design spec for Joe's drill tool** — how analytics should inform which constraint you manipulate. Harjiv Singh co-author. Read this before writing a line of tool code.

- **Allen, T., Wilson, S., Cohen, D. D., & Taberner, M. (2021).** Drill design using the 'control-chaos continuum': Blending science and art during return to sport following knee injury in elite football. *Physical Therapy in Sport*. [doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2021.02.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ptsp.2021.02.011) · `key=YMDUYGMH`
  **Drill design + return to sport, in one paper.** The closest published thing to what Joe wants to do.

- **Otte, F., Yearby, T., & Myszka, S. (2024).** The Role of Skill Acquisition Specialists Within Sports — Why Every High-performance Sports Organization Needs These Experts! · `key=CKYAA7T6`
  **The written case for Joe's niche.** Hand him this early; it tells him the job he wants is a real job.

- **Fransen, J. (2026).** Too Soon for the Big Leagues — We Are Not Quite Ready for a Widespread Integration of Skill Acquisition Specialists in High-Performance Sport. *Journal of Motor Learning and Development*. [doi:10.1123/jmld.2025-0103](https://doi.org/10.1123/jmld.2025-0103) · `key=CBJGJQX5`
  **The rebuttal to Otte above.** Teach both. A practitioner who has only heard the case *for* his niche will fold the first time a physician pushes back.

- **Taberner, M., Allen, T., O'Keefe, J., et al. (2025).** Evolving the Control-Chaos Continuum: Part 1 — Translating Knowledge to Enhance On-Pitch Rehabilitation. *JOSPT*. [doi:10.2519/jospt.2025.13158](https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2025.13158) · `key=Y2Z7QVUU`
  Newer than anything in the SecondBrain briefs. Supersedes the 2020/2022 CCC papers as the current statement.

**Tier 2 — supporting:**

- **Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., et al. (2025).** The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. *Quest*. [doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759](https://doi.org/10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759) · `key=CA2CRR6Z`
  Directly answers "does this drill need a defender?" — a task-constraint decision Joe makes daily.
- **Ryland.** The vision-decision-action cycle and American football drills · `key=VHUXVZ63`
- **Avedesian, J. M., Singh, H., Diekfuss, J. A., et al. (2021).** Loss of Motor Stability After Sports-Related Concussion: Opportunities for Motor Learning Strategies to Reduce Musculoskeletal Injury Risk. *Sports Medicine*. [doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01527-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01527-5) · `key=B47LQF4D`
- **Singh, H., Gokeler, A., & Benjaminse, A. (2021).** Effective Attentional Focus Strategies after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Commentary. *IJSPT*. [doi:10.26603/001c.29848](https://doi.org/10.26603/001c.29848) · `key=EYKZD68B`
- **Glazier, P. (2017).** Towards a Grand Unified Theory of sports performance. *Human Movement Science*. [doi:10.1016/j.humov.2015.08.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2015.08.001) · `key=HNVZFTEH`
- **Tan & Oly.** Introduction to Nonlinear Pedagogy: Coaches as Learning Designers · `key=F7GNYK3J`
- **Thelen, E., & Smith, L.** Dynamic Systems Theories · `key=Z7N28V2Z` — the deep root. Reference only.
- **Harper, D., McBurnie, A., Santos, T., et al. (2022).** Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration. *Sports Medicine*. [doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01693-0](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01693-0) · `key=K4Y2H8S8`

## Knowledge — Harjiv Singh's LinkedIn articles

He publishes short (2–5 min) articles steadily; 6,133 followers. Read on 2026-09-01.
These are practitioner-grade writing, not peer-reviewed — cite as opinion, not evidence.
Most relevant to this mission:

- **"Micro-Dosing Skill: A Motor Learning Perspective"** — small, frequent skill exposures. Directly applicable to an athlete who cannot yet take a full session.
- **"Five Considerations for Modeling the Challenge Point Framework"** — how hard should a task be for this learner right now. **This is the core question the drill-design tool has to answer.**
- **"Constraints Have Weight: The Load of Psychological [Momentum]"** — constraints are not free; each one costs the athlete something.
- **"Three Shifts That Will Redefine Motor Learning in Sport"**
- **"Measurement to Expectation: A Statistical Shift in Sport Science"**
- Also: "Sport Science is Repeating AI's Old Mistakes", "Applying Product Strategy to Sports Science", "Effect Size as a Reliability Proxy in Sparse Datasets", "Is the Smallest Worthwhile Change Still Worthwhile?", "Using Deceleration to Infer Psychological Momentum", "Coordinating Complexity: A Project Management Lens on [Sport Science]".

## Wisdom (Communities)

Unconfirmed with Joe — propose, do not assume. See `NOTES.md`.

- **Harjiv Singh directly.** Eric is a 1st-degree LinkedIn connection with 525+ mutual connections. He is one of the few people working exactly the practice-design-in-rehab seam this course is about, and he answers on LinkedIn. **Cheapest, highest-signal wisdom source available — ahead of any community below.** A specific question (e.g. gap 4, contact reintroduction) beats a general introduction.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Alex Sarama's work on the constraints-led approach and ecological dynamics in basketball:

## Overview

Alex Sarama explores the Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) in basketball, in addition to its underlying theory of ecological dynamics. Sarama's consulting work contributed to the Cleveland Cavaliers' franchise-record 64-win season, and he draws on ecological dynamics and neuroscience to show why traditional training limits player growth.

## Key Theoretical Framework

Sarama discusses the three categories of constraint according to Newell's Constraints Model (1986): individual, task, and environment, discussing how they interact to shape every movement we see on the court.

Self-organization is the idea that basketball players organize their bodies naturally to solve movement problems, while perception-action coupling is the idea that perception informs action, and action is always shaping perception.

## Practical Application

The Constraints-Led Approach is an evidence-based methodology that replaces outdated repetitive drills with practice environments mirroring real-game unpredictability. Sarama provides practical examples of how to implement the CLA with players of all levels, from beginners to the NBA and WNBA.

## Publications and Resources

Sarama authored "Transforming Basketball: A Constraints-Led Approach to Basketball Performance," now in its Second Edition. His work has been adopted by coaches at all levels of the game, with the delivery of coaching clinics and player camps in over 40 countries.

## Ecological Approach & Philosophy

Alex Sarama's evidence-informed coaching ideas are based upon the Constraint Led Approach (CLA) underpinned by Ecological Dynamics (EcoD). Sarama has been conducting research and practical applications since 2016 focused on the principles of human movement science, ecological psychology, dynamics systems theory and complex systems.

## NBA & Professional Credentials

He consults for NBA, NCAA and professional teams, while also serving as Player Improvement Specialist for Paris Basketball in the EuroCup and Head Coach of College Prep in Borgomanero, Italy. He previously worked for the Cleveland Cavaliers, NBA Europe based in Madrid, as well as Paris Basketball in the EuroCup and the Rip City Remix (the Portland Trail Blazers' G League Affiliate).

## Current Position & Background

Alex is currently Head Coach for the Portland Fire in the WNBA. Only 30 years old, the majority of his coaching journey has taken place overseas (He is British).

# Alex Sarama and the Portland Fire's Constraints-Led Approach

## About Alex Sarama

Sarama is the first-year head coach of the Portland Fire expansion team and is described as "a leading expert" in the Constraints-Led Approach (CLA). He meticulously documents his communication with players, recording himself during huddles and practices to review his clarity and messaging at day's end.

## The CLA Training Method

CLA emphasizes practicing with variability through game-like situations with intentional obstacles. Rather than repetitive drills, players learn to adapt by solving problems—"knowing the shot you are supposed to take, but with different obstacles in the way."

Specific examples include:
- Shooting with five different ball sizes and textures
- Practicing finishing with restricted hand placement and footwork
- Practicing in socks to limit jumping and explore unfamiliar movement patterns
- Rotating players in four-minute bursts followed by rest periods

Sarama stated: "We actually want to avoid randomness at all costs," emphasizing the approach has structure despite appearances.

## Absence of Rehabilitation/Medical Content

The article contains **no information** about injury rehabilitation, load management, sports medicine, or return-to-play protocols.

The only criticism mentioned comes implicitly from observers around the league: "for some people who have been around the WNBA for 30 years, it seemed unserious," referring to the sock-practice video. However, no direct quotes expressing skepticism appear in the article.

# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. None written yet. |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. Created lazily at the first record. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.

He is real and he is big. But not for what you need.

content.text:
Checked the extractor. It cuts the PDF **by page number**, not by chapter. That decides it.

## Short answer: front to back, one file

Scan the **whole book in order into one PDF**. Here is why.

The ingest tool asks for page ranges, like "pages 40 to 62." It has no idea what a chapter is. So the page numbers in the file have to match the real book. If you hand me five separate chapter files, page 1 of file 3 is really page 87 — and every page number I cite in a lesson would be wrong. Your handoff says lessons must cite real page numbers.

Also, the tool **already goes one chapter at a time by itself**, and saves its place after each one. So you get the chapter-by-chapter benefit for free. You do not need to do that part by hand.

## But scan in batches anyway

Do not try to do 300 pages in one sitting. Scan 30 or 40 pages at a time so you never lose much if something goes wrong. Just keep them **in order** and name them so they sort:

```
part-01.pdf, part-02.pdf, part-03.pdf ...
```

I made you a folder to drop them in:


When you are done, tell me and I will merge them and run OCR. Or do it yourself:

```
cd /Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/scans
qpdf --empty --pages part-*.pdf -- merged.pdf
ocrmypdf --skip-text merged.pdf ../myszka-book.pdf
```

## Four rules while you scan

1. **Do not skip pages.** Not the blank ones, not the picture ones. One missing page shifts every page number after it, and my citations go wrong from there on.
2. **Include the front matter**, especially the **table of contents**. That is how I build the chapter map. Without it I have to guess where chapters start.
3. **300 dpi or better.** Grayscale is fine, colour is not needed. Low resolution gives bad OCR, and bad OCR puts wrong words in your quotes.
4. **Do not OCR the batches.** OCR once at the very end, on the merged file.

## Types of Constraints

Task Constraints involve the rules of the game (e.g., changing rules, modifying scoring systems, altering playing areas, adjusting shot clocks), Environmental Constraints relate to the physical space (e.g., gym noise, lighting, floor type, or even playing outdoors), and Individual Constraints encompass the player's unique traits (e.g., players' skill level, physical traits, motivation, fatigue, etc.)

## Practical Examples of Task Constraints

From Transforming Basketball resources, some practical constraint examples include:

- An advantage game where coaches can call turnovers if players do not shoot, pass or drive in less than one second to encourage quick decisions
- Fortnite scoring involving a team needing to score off 1 reject, 1 slip, 1 ghost screen and 1 advance pass to win an activity
- The Joker constraint where one player can earn a bonus point for their team off every screen or pass assist
- Playing shorter games where the winning team must make 4 out of 5 free throws to seal the win or avoid a consequence

## Key Coaching Principles

Coaches should purposefully manipulate task constraints to invite potential movement solutions to emerge, and coaches have to be very careful to refrain from over-constraining players, which happens by too heavily restricting the behaviors or solutions players can use.

# Newell's Constraints Model Definition and Examples

## The Three Categories

According to the article, Newell's Constraints Model (1986) identifies three types of constraints that shape movement behavior:

1. **Individual**: "Player-specific factors"
2. **Environmental**: "Physical and socio-cultural factors"
3. **Task**: "Specific to the activity or game"

The piece notes that coaches have the most direct control over task constraints when designing small-sided games.

---

## Practical Constraint Examples by Category

### Task Constraints
- Shot clock (6-second limit to speed decision-making)
- Shot selection rules (non-ROB shots result in turnovers; lay-ups worth double points)
- Dribble limits (maximum 2 dribbles)
- Scoring modifications (altered point values for different shot types)
- Defense rewards (blocked shots worth 4 points)
- Turnovers for specific infractions (catching ball in "lava," failing to react appropriately)
- Individualized scoring bonuses ("Golden scorer," "Assist king/queen" systems)
- Different closeout types (hot, cold, normal)
- Varied starting positions for defenders

### Environmental Constraints
- Music
- Simulated crowd noises
- Communication restrictions ("No verbals")

### Individual Constraints
- Fatigue management (alternating full-court and half-court games)
- Varied opponent types (taller, shorter, faster, slower defenders)
- Position-specific scoring bonuses

content.content:
# The 5 Principles of the Constraints-Led Approach

## 1. **Representative Learning Design (RLD)**
Practice environments should mirror actual game conditions. "Does it look—and feel—like the game?" Players need authentic perception-action coupling, meaning they must make real decisions with defenders and teammates present. Isolated drills without game-like constraints won't transfer to competition.

## 2. **Manipulation of Constraints**
Coaches design "boundaries" to guide players toward desired behaviors rather than telling them what to do. These fall into three categories: task constraints (rule modifications, shot clocks), environmental constraints (gym conditions), and individual constraints (player skill levels). When you're constantly yelling instructions, "you have a design problem"—the constraints aren't providing enough feedback.

## 3. **External Focus of Attention**
Give players outcome-focused cues rather than body mechanics instructions. Instead of "bend your knees," try "aim for a BRAD (Back Rim and Down)." Research shows internal focus actually disrupts fluid movement, while external cues targeting environmental effects enhance performance.

## 4. **Task Simplification**
Reduce problem complexity while keeping perception and action together. Rather than removing defense entirely, reduce defensive pressure so players can still "read" the environment. Use equipment scaling or reduce player numbers (3v1 instead of 5v5) to make solutions more obvious.

## 5. **Functional Variability**
Encourage movement exploration rather than one "perfect technique." Players should find solutions that work for their unique abilities. Success means solving the problem, not achieving textbook form—players in games never execute identically twice.

Think of it as two layers, not one question.

## Two things on the site that fight how rehab drills are normally built

This is the good stuff.

**1. "Reduce the pressure, don't remove the defender."** In rehab the reflex is to strip a drill down to nobody guarding. The argument on that page is that this does not make the task simpler — it deletes the task. You took away the very reading the athlete needs to get back.

Careful here: **that rehab twist is mine, not theirs.** They said it about beginners, not injured players. I have flagged that in the files so nobody quotes them saying it. The real citation is Parry (2025), already in your Zotero.

# Ecological Dynamics in Musculoskeletal Rehab: Analysis

## Author & Credentials
**Yuji** (last name not provided in article) is a licensed chiropractor and certified strength and conditioning specialist based in Portland, Oregon. He applies ecological dynamics framework principles to pain management and performance coaching.

## Core Arguments

The article argues against traditional tissue-focused rehabilitation models. Instead, it advocates for an **enactivism and affordances-based approach** that considers the entire person-environment system rather than isolated anatomical issues.

Key premise: "Affordances are described as opportunities for action offered by the environment" (Gibson, 1979). The individual's perception of these opportunities depends on their current physical state, intentions, and environmental context.

## Application to Injured Patients

**Constraints Model**: Pain and injury create "organism constraints"—reduced range of motion, strength, self-efficacy, fear, and attention focus. These alterations change a person's "field of affordances," limiting perceived movement options.

**Example**: A well-rested powerlifter and a fatigued person with back pain facing identical boxes perceive different lifting possibilities. The injured person might only perceive pushing or ignoring affordances rather than lifting.

**Perception-Action Coupling**: The article emphasizes that "perceiving-cognizing-acting are inseparable" and continuously guide behavior contextually.

## Recommended Practice Changes

Rather than repetitive exercises targeting isolated capacities, clinicians should:

- Design variable, naturalistic practice environments reflecting real-world demands
- Cultivate patient problem-solving rather than perfect movement patterns
- Foster "dexterity"—the ability to adaptively respond to environmental changes
- Close the gap between artificial clinical settings and performance environments

## Key References

Eight peer-reviewed sources cited, including Vaz et al. (2023), Stilwell & Harman (2019), and foundational work by Gibson (1979) and Bernstein (1996).

# Analysis of "Part 2 - Opportunities in Clinical Practice"

## Author Information

The article is written by **Rich White**, though the byline identifies him as a guest contributor. The author bio at the end identifies the actual writer as **Yuji**, a licensed chiropractor and certified strength and conditioning specialist based in Portland, Oregon. Yuji's credentials include expertise in pain science and ecological dynamics frameworks for movement.

## Core Practical Opportunities

The article presents three main themes for clinical practice:

1. **Accepting variability and encouraging exploration**
2. **Keeping perception and action coupled**
3. **Coaching to guide problem-solving**

## Key Premise on Exercise Design

Rather than drilling a single "perfect" movement pattern, clinicians should present what the author calls "alive movement problems." The fundamental shift involves: "repeat the process of finding a solution" rather than "rote repetition" of identical movements.

## Concrete Constraint Manipulation Examples

Clinicians can modify lifting activities through:
- Various implements (dumbbells, kettlebells, medicine balls)
- Different starting heights and target heights
- Variable foot positions and grip widths
- Time constraints and fatigue levels
- Environmental factors (lighting, flooring, temperature)
- Social context (exercising near others)

## Critical Principle

"Change the nuanced parameters for a movement problem without changing the global nature" allows practitioners to create variability while maintaining safety boundaries based on pain and tissue capacity thresholds.

## Warm-Up Application

Novel, task-based activities during warm-ups can prime problem-solving through activities like ball rolls, dowel touches, and floor getups—allowing patients to practice "thoughtless, fearless movements."

## Key References Cited

- Bernstein (1967) - coordination and regulation
- Cholewicki et al. (2019) - multifactorial nature of low back pain
- Davids et al. (2003) - movement systems as dynamical systems
- Edelman & Gally (2001) - degeneracy in biological systems
- Myszka, Yearby, & Davids (2023a, 2023b) - problem-solving and dexterity

# Analysis of "Injury and Affordance Perception"

## Author & Credentials

**Javier Miler-Estrada** is co-founder of Ignite Performance in Chandler, Arizona, a premier training facility specializing in youth-to-professional athlete development. The facility has helped over 100 athletes obtain college scholarships.

## Core Argument

The article critiques traditional biomechanical approaches to rehabilitation, proposing instead an **ecological dynamics framework** where injury affects how athletes perceive action opportunities in their environment.

**Key thesis:** "Affordances are opportunities for action that are both athlete and frame-dependent" (Gibson, 1979). Injury fundamentally alters this perception.

### How Injury Changes Affordance Perception

Miler-Estrada argues injury creates psychological and perceptual barriers:

- Injury history influences what movements athletes believe are possible
- A rugby player with previous shoulder dislocation may unconsciously avoid using that limb in tackles, limiting available tactical solutions
- The author notes: "anxiety causes subjects to underestimate their action capabilities, which suggests anxiety affects the perception of affordances"

Athletes become trapped in constrained movement patterns rather than accessing their full adaptive potential.

## Return-to-Play/Performance Recommendations

The article advocates **gradual exposure to sport-relevant complexity:**

1. **Progressive contextualization**: Rather than isolated exercises, embed athletes in "alive movement problems" progressively mimicking competitive conditions

2. **Redirect attentional focus**: Move athletes away from internal biomechanical monitoring ("avoid knee valgus") toward environmental problem-solving

3. **Incremental stress exposure**: Introduce anxiety and variability systematically rather than shielding athletes in controlled settings

4. **Sport-specific problem design**: "Design an activity where the athlete has to catch or 'high point' a ball and then land safely" rather than prescribing "perfect" isolated movements

The case study illustrates this: an ACL-injured football player progressed from facility-based training to field sessions with realistic opponents and equipment, expanding his perceived affordances progressively.

# 5 Principles for Effective Ecological Coaching

## 1. The Performer-Environment Relationship

**Principle:** "The performer-environment relationship is reciprocal or mutual, where energy is exchanged."

Energy flows between performer and environment, creating opportunities for action called affordances. These perceived opportunities depend on the individual's current action capabilities. Coaches should analyze behavior at the scale of the performer-environment system to understand how movers solve problems in their performance context.

## Rob Gray's Background and Research

Rob Gray is a professor at Arizona State University who has been conducting research on and teaching courses related to perceptual-motor skill for over 25 years. He completed his master's and doctoral degrees in experimental psychology at York University in Canada, and after receiving his doctorate in 1998, he worked as a research scientist for Nissan Motor Corporation in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

## Research on Injury Recovery

His research has focused on understanding perceptual-motor control in sports and applying that knowledge to help athletes acquire skills faster and reduce performance issues associated with things like pressure and injury recovery. ABSTRACTNOTE: Background/Objectives: Differential learning (DL) amplifies natural fluctuations in movement execution and, in its more extreme forms, facilitates repetition-free training with minimal external feedback. It is also a free, on-mission written source, and it is the only place found so far where the ecological-dynamics people write directly about injured people.** Run by **Shawn Myszka and Tyler Yearby** — two of the four practitioners and two of the three textbook authors. [Blog index](https://emergentmvmt.com/emergence-blog/)

**Three posts sit on the rehab seam.** They are practitioner writing, not peer-reviewed — cite as opinion — but they are **reference-backed**, which puts them above most blog content.

- **["Ecological Dynamics in Musculoskeletal Rehab"](https://emergentmvmt.com/ecological-dynamics-in-musculoskeletal-rehab/)** (May 2024) — by **Yuji**, a chiropractor and CSCS in Portland, OR. The argument against tissue-focused rehab. **The idea worth stealing: pain and injury are *organism constraints*.** Reduced range, weakness, fear, low self-efficacy and narrowed attention all shrink the athlete's **"field of affordances"** — the set of actions they can even perceive as available. His worked contrast: a rested powerlifter and a fatigued person with back pain look at the same box and perceive different possibilities. **This gives Joe a single mechanism that ties the medical facts to the performance problem.** Cites Gibson (1979), Bernstein (1996), Stilwell & Harman (2019), Vaz et al. (2023).
- **["Part 2 — Opportunities in Clinical Practice"](https://emergentmvmt.com/part-2-opportunities-in-clinical-practice/)** (Aug 2024) — the practical half. Three moves: **accept variability and encourage exploration · keep perception and action coupled · coach to guide problem-solving.** Its best single line for a clinician: **"change the nuanced parameters of a movement problem without changing its global nature"** — that is how you get variability while staying inside pain and tissue-capacity limits, and it is a direct answer to the safety objection Joe will face. Includes a concrete constraint list for loaded work (implement, start height, target height, foot position, grip, time pressure, fatigue, lighting, flooring, social context). Cites Bernstein (1967), Davids et al. (2003), Edelman & Gally (2001), Myszka/Yearby/Davids (2023).
  **Byline warning:** the post is bylined **Rich White** but the author bio at the foot names **Yuji**. **Resolve who wrote it before citing either name.**
- **["Injury and Affordance Perception"](https://emergentmvmt.com/injury-and-affordance-perception/)** (Apr 2023) — by **Javier Miler-Estrada**, co-founder of Ignite Performance (Chandler, AZ). **The closest thing found to a written RTP progression in this tradition**, and it ends in an **ACL case study of a football player** moving from facility work to field sessions against real opponents. Its four moves: progressive contextualisation · **redirect attention off the body part** ("avoid knee valgus" is the wrong cue) · **introduce anxiety and variability deliberately rather than shielding the athlete** · design sport-specific problems ("catch or high-point a ball, then land safely"). **Note the claim that anxiety makes athletes underestimate their own action capabilities** — that is the same mechanism as the Gray paper below.

**Also worth reading, not rehab:** **["5 Principles for Effective Ecological Coaching"](https://emergentmvmt.com/5-principles-for-effective-ecological-coaching/)** by **Tyler Yearby** — a course pillar writing the framework in plain language, free. Performer–environment reciprocity · alive movement problems · constraining to afford · repetition without repetition · movement ownership. **Better first reading for Joe than any journal paper in this file, and it is by the lead author of the anchor paper.** Note principle 5's caveat: intervene when a pattern is **non-functional or injury-prone** — the clearest statement of where their approach concedes ground to a clinician.

**The organisation also runs:** the **Adaptable Athlete Podcast**, the **Sport Movement Skill Conference**, and a **Certified Skill Acquisition Specialist (CSAS)** credential. **The CSAS is a career lever for Joe, not just reading** — pair it with Otte (2024) (`CKYAA7T6`), the written case for his niche, and its rebuttal Fransen (2026) (`CBJGJQX5`). Prices are not listed publicly; ask before assuming it is affordable.

Checked 2026-09-02, because "Rob Gray" is easy to file as a generic ecological-dynamics name. **He is not that. He is an experimental psychologist (PhD), Associate Professor at ASU, with a top paper near 900 citations** — the most rigorously credentialed of the four practitioners. **But his research base is attention, choking under pressure, virtual-reality transfer and baseball batting — not rehabilitation.** Most-cited: attention and choking in complex skill (2004), focus of attention in baseball batting (2007), transfer from virtual to real batting (2017).

# The Perception & Action Podcast: Overview

## Site Purpose
This is a podcast and educational platform focused on "how psychological research can be applied to improving performance, accelerating skill acquisition & designing technologies."

## Main Sections
- **Home, About, Episodes, Journal Club, Resources**
- **Books** - Available but specific titles not detailed
- **Consulting/Speaking** - Professional services offered
- **Courses** - Including a new "Dynamical Systems Theory in Coaching" certification course
- **Support** - Patreon and PayPal options for funding

## Podcast & Distribution
Available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Google Podcasts, Amazon Music, and YouTube. Hosted by Rob Gray.

## Content Focus Areas
Recent episodes emphasize:
- **Practice Design**: Using analytics to inform training approaches
- **Constraints**: "Why do we constrain?" and how constraints affect movement behavior
- **Ecological Dynamics**: Addressing misconceptions about this coaching framework
- **Representative Design**: Evaluating practice authenticity

Episode 584 specifically addresses "what if the way we train young athletes is stealing the very talent we are trying to develop?"

## Pricing
No pricing shown for courses, books, or services on this page.

## Host
Rob Gray runs the platform and produces content.

# PACE Courses Overview

## Available Courses

### 1. Practice Design and Adaptation with the Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) Certification
**Price:** $1,995 USD ($399 upfront, then $399/month)
**Duration:** ~4 months
**Max Enrollment:** 8 students
**Instructor:** Rob Gray

This program teaches coaches to use the CLA method, covering "initial practice design, using performance analytics to support design, scaling constraints to optimize challenge" and related skills. The course combines self-paced online material, optional group webinars, and one-on-one meetings. Learners submit practice videos for feedback and must complete a final quiz to earn certification.

**Status:** Winter and Spring 2027 sessions are full; waitlist available.

---

### 2. Applying Dynamical Systems Theory in Coaching Certification
**Price:** $1,995 USD ($399 upfront, then $399/month)
**Duration:** ~4 months (16 weeks active + 4 weeks for completion)
**Max Enrollment:** 8 students
**Instructor:** Rob Gray

This course teaches coaches to "measure and use what matters in performance" through observational techniques, IMU sensor data collection, and camera-based analysis. Topics include coordination dynamics, complexity measures, entropy, kinematic sequencing, and interpersonal synchrony. No coding experience required.

**Status:** First session enrolling now (starts February 1, 2027)

Both courses award digital certification upon completion.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-video/watch/0.2.0/skills/watch

# /watch

You don't have a video input; this skill gives you one. A Python script gets captions first, optionally downloads the video, extracts frames as JPEGs (scene-aware, or fast keyframes at `efficient` detail), gets a timestamped transcript (native captions first, then Whisper API as fallback), and prints frame paths. You then `Read` each frame path to see the images and combine them with the transcript to answer the user.

## Resolve `SKILL_DIR` (do this before any command)

Every `python3 ...` command below runs a bundled script under `SKILL_DIR/scripts/`. Set `SKILL_DIR` to the **absolute path of the directory containing THIS SKILL.md you just Read** — your harness told you that path in the Read result. The scripts are always a direct sibling of this file (`SKILL_DIR/scripts/watch.py`), in every install layout:

```
Read ~/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-video/watch/<ver>/skills/watch/SKILL.md → SKILL_DIR=…/skills/watch
Read ~/.codex/skills/watch/SKILL.md                                          → SKILL_DIR=~/.codex/skills/watch
Read ~/.agents/skills/watch/SKILL.md                                         → SKILL_DIR=~/.agents/skills/watch
```

Substitute that literal path for `${SKILL_DIR}` in every command. This works on every harness (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, …) without relying on any harness-specific environment variable. Guard once at the start of a run:

```bash
SKILL_DIR="<absolute path of the directory containing the SKILL.md you Read>"
if [ ! -f "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/watch.py" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: scripts/watch.py not found under SKILL_DIR=$SKILL_DIR" >&2
  echo "Re-check the directory of the SKILL.md you Read and substitute it as SKILL_DIR." >&2
  exit 1
fi
```

## Step 0 — Setup preflight (runs every `/watch` invocation, silent on success)

**Python interpreter:** every `python3 ...` command in this skill is for macOS/Linux. On **Windows**, substitute `python` — the `python3` command on Windows is the Microsoft Store stub and will not run the script.

On the first `/watch` invocation in a session, use structured preflight so you can detect first-run setup:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --json
```

Branch on two fields:

- **`can_proceed: true` and `first_run: false`** → setup is already done (the user may have deliberately skipped a Whisper key — that's allowed). Proceed to Step 1 without comment.
- **`first_run: true`** → genuine first-time setup. Do these in order:
  1. If `missing_binaries` is non-empty, run the installer first (it auto-installs on macOS / prints commands elsewhere — see below) and confirm the binaries land. **Do not skip this and jump to preferences.**
  2. Run the installer once more if needed so it scaffolds `~/.config/watch/.env` (it only writes the template when the file is absent, so let it create the file *before* you write any values into it).
  3. Encourage a Whisper API key and ask the watch-preference questions below, then write the selected values into `~/.config/watch/.env` and set `SETUP_COMPLETE=true`.
- **`can_proceed: false` and `first_run: false`** → setup was finished before but the environment regressed (e.g. `missing_binaries` after an OS change). Run the installer to remediate, then proceed. Don't re-ask preferences.

A missing Whisper key is *encouraged to fix, not required*: on a genuine first run `status` will read `needs_key` even when binaries are present — that's your cue to encourage a key, not a blocker.

On follow-up `/watch` calls in the same session, use the silent check:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --check
```

This is a <100ms lookup. Exit 0 means /watch can run — this **includes a user who finished setup without a Whisper key** (keyless is allowed). On exit 0 the script emits **nothing** — proceed to Step 1 without comment. **Do NOT announce "setup is complete" to the user** — they don't need a status message on every turn. The only acceptable user-visible output from Step 0 is when remediation is required.

On non-zero exit, follow the table:

| Exit | Meaning | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| `2` | Missing binaries (`ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` / `yt-dlp`) | Run installer |
| `3` | Genuine first run with no Whisper API key | Run installer to scaffold `.env`, then encourage a key (the user may decline — proceed with `--no-whisper`) |
| `4` | Both missing | Run installer, then encourage a key |

Exit `3` only fires before the user has completed setup. Once `SETUP_COMPLETE=true` is written, a keyless install returns exit 0 and is never nagged again.

The installer is idempotent — safe to re-run:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py"
```

On macOS with Homebrew, it auto-installs `ffmpeg` and `yt-dlp`. On Linux/Windows, it prints the exact install commands for the user to run. It scaffolds `~/.config/watch/.env` with commented placeholders and default watch settings at `0600` perms.

**If an API key is still missing after install:** use `AskUserQuestion` to ask the user whether they have a Groq API key (preferred — cheaper, faster) or an OpenAI key. Then write it into `~/.config/watch/.env` — set the matching `GROQ_API_KEY=...` or `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` line. If they don't want to set up Whisper, proceed with `--no-whisper` and tell them videos without native captions will come back frames-only.

**First-run watch preference:** after the installer has scaffolded `~/.config/watch/.env`, use `AskUserQuestion` to ask one question:

- Default detail (one dial). Present these as `AskUserQuestion` options in this exact order — lightest to heaviest — and keep `(recommended)` on `balanced` even though it is not first (do **not** reorder to put the recommended option first):
  - `transcript` — no frames at all, transcript only (skips video download when captions exist).
  - `efficient` — fast keyframe pass (cap 50).
  - `balanced` (recommended) — scene-aware frames (cap 100, default).
  - `token-burner` — scene-aware, uncapped (maximum fidelity; high token cost).

Write the answer directly into `~/.config/watch/.env` by setting the bare key on its own line — **no trailing inline comment** (a `# note` after the value can break parsing):

```bash
WATCH_DETAIL=balanced
```

Use the user's selected value. If they skip the question, keep the recommended default. Once dependencies, the API-key choice, and this preference are handled, write or update `SETUP_COMPLETE=true` in the same file. Do not ask this preference question again when `SETUP_COMPLETE=true`.

**Structured mode (optional):** `python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --json` emits `{status, can_proceed, first_run, setup_complete, missing_binaries, whisper_backend, has_api_key, config_file, watch_detail, platform}` where `status` is one of `ready | needs_install | needs_key | needs_install_and_key`. `status` describes the *ideal* state (a key is encouraged, so a keyless first run reads `needs_key`); `can_proceed` is the operational gate (binaries present AND a key is set OR setup was already completed). Branch on `can_proceed`/`first_run` to decide whether to run; use `status` to decide what to encourage.

Within a single session, you can skip Step 0 on follow-up `/watch` calls — once `--check` returned 0, nothing about the environment changes between turns.

## When to use

- User pastes a video URL (YouTube, Vimeo, X, TikTok, Twitch clip, most yt-dlp-supported sites) and asks about it.
- User points at a local video file (`.mp4`, `.mov`, `.mkv`, `.webm`, etc.) and asks about it.
- User types `/watch <url-or-path> [question]`.

## Recommended limits

- **Best accuracy: videos under 10 minutes.** Frame coverage scales inversely with duration.
- **Universal rate cap: 2 fps.** The script never samples faster than 2 fps, even when a budget or `--fps` would imply more.
- **The frame ceiling is set by the detail mode** (`WATCH_DETAIL` in `~/.config/watch/.env`, or `--detail`), not a single global cap:
  - `transcript` → no frames
  - `efficient` → up to **50** (keyframes)
  - `balanced` (default) → up to **100** (scene-aware)
  - `token-burner` → **uncapped** (scene-aware; a soft warning prints past 250 frames)
  - `--max-frames N` overrides whichever cap the mode would otherwise use.
- **Full-video frame budget by duration.** Token cost grows with frame count, so the script targets a budget by duration. This budget sets the fps and the uniform-sampling fallback; scene-aware selection can fill up to the detail cap above, whichever is lower:
  - ≤30s → ~12-30 frames
  - 30s-1min → ~40 frames
  - 1-3min → ~60 frames
  - 3-10min → ~80 frames
  - \>10min → up to the detail cap, sparsely spaced (warning printed)
- If the user hands you a long video, consider asking whether they want a specific section before burning tokens on a sparse scan.

## How to invoke

**Step 1 — parse the user input.** Separate the video source (URL or path) from any question the user asked. Example: `/watch https://youtu.be/abc what language is this in?` → source = `https://youtu.be/abc`, question = `what language is this in?`.

**Step 2 — run the watch script.** Pass the source verbatim. Do not shell-escape it yourself beyond normal quoting:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "<source>"
```

Optional flags:
- `--detail transcript|efficient|balanced|token-burner` — fidelity/speed dial. `transcript` = no frames (transcript only, skips video download when captions exist); `efficient` = fast keyframes (cap 50); `balanced` = scene-aware frames (cap 100); `token-burner` = scene-aware, uncapped.
- `--start T` / `--end T` — focus on a section. Accepts `SS`, `MM:SS`, or `HH:MM:SS`. When either is set, fps auto-scales denser (see "Focusing on a section" below).
- `--timestamps T1,T2,…` — grab a frame at each of these absolute timestamps (`SS`, `MM:SS`, or `HH:MM:SS`). Use this after reading the transcript to capture deictic moments the presenter flags ("look here", "as you can see", "notice this") that visual selection alone may miss. See "Transcript-cue frames" below.
- `--max-frames N` — override the preset cap for tighter token budget (e.g. `--max-frames 40`)
- `--resolution W` — change frame width in px (default 512; bump to 1024 only if the user needs to read on-screen text)
- `--fps F` — override auto-fps (clamped to 2 fps max)
- `--out-dir DIR` — keep working files somewhere specific (default: an auto-generated tmp dir)
- `--whisper groq|openai` — force a specific Whisper backend (default: prefer Groq if both keys exist)
- `--no-whisper` — disable the Whisper fallback entirely (frames-only if no captions)
- `--no-dedup` — keep near-duplicate frames. By default a frame-delta pass drops frames that are visually near-identical to the previous kept one (held slides, static screen recordings, paused video) so the frame budget goes to distinct content; the report's **Frames** line notes how many were dropped. Pass this only if the user needs every sampled frame (e.g. judging subtle frame-to-frame motion).

### Focusing on a section (higher frame rate)

When the user asks about a specific moment — "what happens at the 2 minute mark?", "zoom into 0:45 to 1:00", "the first 10 seconds" — pass `--start` and/or `--end`. The script switches to focused-mode budgets, which are denser than full-video budgets (still capped at 2 fps, and still bounded by the detail-mode cap — the counts below assume the default `balanced` cap of 100; `efficient` tops out at 50):

- ≤5s → 2 fps (up to 10 frames)
- 5-15s → 2 fps (up to 30 frames)
- 15-30s → ~2 fps (up to 60 frames)
- 30-60s → ~1.3 fps (up to 80 frames)
- 60-180s → ~0.6 fps (100 frames, capped)

Focused mode is the right call for:
- Any moment/range the user names explicitly ("around 2:30", "the intro", "the last 30 seconds").
- Any video longer than ~10 minutes where the user's question is about a specific part — running focused on the relevant section is far more useful than a sparse scan of the whole thing.
- Re-runs after a full scan didn't have enough detail in some region.

Transcript is auto-filtered to the same range. Frame timestamps are absolute (real video timeline, not offset-from-start).

Examples:
```bash
# Last 10 seconds of a 1 minute video
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" video.mp4 --start 50 --end 60

# Zoom into 2:15 → 2:45 at 2 fps (60 frames)
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "$URL" --start 2:15 --end 2:45 --fps 2

# From 1h12m to the end of the video
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "$URL" --start 1:12:00
```

**Step 3 — Read every frame path the script lists.** The Read tool renders JPEGs directly as images for you. Read all frames in a single message (parallel tool calls) so you see them together. The frames are in chronological order with a `t=MM:SS` timestamp so you can align them to the transcript.

**Step 4 — answer the user.** You now have two streams of evidence:
- **Frames** — what's on screen at each timestamp
- **Transcript** — what's said at each timestamp. The report's header shows the source (`captions` = yt-dlp pulled native subs; `whisper (groq)` or `whisper (openai)` = transcribed by API).

If the user asked a specific question, answer it directly citing timestamps. If they didn't ask anything, summarize what happens in the video — structure, key moments, notable visuals, spoken content.

This holds for `transcript` detail too: even with no frames, produce a **summary** like the other modes — do not paste the full transcript into chat. Synthesize structure, key moments, and spoken content with timestamps; quote only the lines that matter. Offer the raw transcript only if the user explicitly asks for it.

**Step 5 — clean up.** The script prints a working directory at the end. If the user isn't going to ask follow-ups about this video, delete it with `rm -rf <dir>`. If they might, leave it in place.

## Detail and frames

Default behavior comes from `~/.config/watch/.env`:

- `WATCH_DETAIL=transcript|efficient|balanced|token-burner` (default: `balanced`)

At `transcript` detail, captions are enough to return a report without downloading video. If captions are missing, the script downloads audio only and tries Whisper. If no transcript can be produced, it reports the limitation clearly; re-run with `--detail balanced` for frames.

At `efficient` detail, the script downloads the video and extracts **keyframes only** (`ffmpeg -skip_frame nokey`) — a near-instant pass that lands frames on scene cuts. If a clip has fewer than 4 keyframes it falls back to uniform sampling.

At `balanced` / `token-burner` detail, the script extracts **scene-aware** frames: ffmpeg scene-change selection first, falling back to uniform sampling only when the video is effectively static. `balanced` caps at 100 frames; `token-burner` is uncapped. Frame report lines include both timestamp and selection reason. Extracted images are clamped to a maximum 1998px height for Claude Read compatibility.

## Transcript-cue frames

Visual frame selection (scene/keyframe) can miss the moments a presenter explicitly flags — "look here", "as you can see", "notice this", "watch what happens" — because pointing at a slide is often a *low* visual change. `--timestamps` lets you force a frame at those exact moments. **You** decide which moments matter, by reading the transcript:

1. Run once at `--detail transcript` (or any detail) to get the timestamped transcript.
2. Scan it for deictic cues — phrases where the speaker directs attention to something on screen. This is a judgment call (ignore rhetorical "look, the point is…"); that's why it's done by you, not a regex.
3. Re-run with `--timestamps 4:32,7:10,9:55` (absolute source times). For a URL, point the second run at the **downloaded local file** in the work dir so it doesn't re-download.

Behavior:
- **Additive by default.** Cue frames (`reason=transcript-cue`) are merged into whatever `--detail` already selected, in chronological order.
- **Pinned and counted first.** Cue frames are reserved against the frame cap before the detail engine runs, so they're never evicted by even-sampling.
- **Honors focus mode.** With `--start/--end`, any cue timestamp outside the window is dropped (reported in the summary). Coordinates are always absolute source time.
- **Cue-only frames.** `--detail transcript --timestamps …` skips scene/keyframe sampling and returns *only* the cue frames (it will download the video to do so, since frames need pixels).

## Transcription

The script gets a timestamped transcript in one of two ways:

1. **Native captions (free, preferred).** yt-dlp pulls manual or auto-generated subtitles from the source platform if available.
2. **Whisper API fallback.** If no captions came back (or the source is a local file), the script extracts audio (`ffmpeg -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 -b:a 64k`, ~0.5 MB/min) and uploads it to whichever Whisper API has a key configured:
   - **Groq** — `whisper-large-v3`. Preferred default: cheaper, faster. Get a key at console.groq.com/keys.
   - **OpenAI** — `whisper-1`. Fallback. Get a key at platform.openai.com/api-keys.

Both keys live in `~/.config/watch/.env`. The script prefers Groq when both are set; override with `--whisper openai` to force OpenAI. Use `--no-whisper` to skip the fallback entirely.

## Failure modes and handling

- **Setup preflight failed** → run `python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py"` (auto-installs ffmpeg/yt-dlp via brew on macOS, scaffolds the `.env`). For API key, ask the user via `AskUserQuestion` and write it to `~/.config/watch/.env`.
- **No transcript available** → captions missing AND (no Whisper key OR Whisper API failed). Script prints a hint pointing to setup. Proceed frames-only and tell the user.
- **Long video warning printed** → acknowledge it in your answer. Offer to re-run focused on a specific section via `--start`/`--end` rather than a sparse full-video scan.
- **Download fails** → yt-dlp's error goes to stderr. If it's a login-required or region-locked video, tell the user plainly; do not keep retrying.
- **Whisper request fails** → the error is printed to stderr (likely: invalid key or rate limit). Audio over the API's 25 MB upload cap is split into chunks and transcribed automatically, so length alone won't fail it; if some chunks fail the transcript is partial and the dropped chunks are noted on stderr. The report will say "none available" only if every chunk fails. You can retry with `--whisper openai` if Groq failed (or vice versa).

## Token efficiency

This skill burns tokens primarily on frames. Order of magnitude:
- 80 frames at 512px wide is roughly 50-80k image tokens depending on aspect ratio.
- The transcript is cheap (a few thousand tokens at most for a 10-minute video).
- Bumping `--resolution` to 1024 roughly quadruples the image tokens per frame. Only do it when necessary.

If you already watched a video this session and the user asks a follow-up, do **not** re-run the script — you already have the frames and transcript in context. Just answer from what you have.

## Security & Permissions

**What this skill does:**
- Runs `yt-dlp` locally to download the video and pull native captions when the source supports them (public data; the request goes directly to whatever host the URL points at)
- Runs `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` locally to extract frames as JPEGs and, when Whisper is needed, a mono 16 kHz audio clip
- Sends the extracted audio clip to Groq's Whisper API (`api.groq.com/openai/v1/audio/transcriptions`) when `GROQ_API_KEY` is set (preferred — cheaper, faster)
- Sends the extracted audio clip to OpenAI's audio transcription API (`api.openai.com/v1/audio/transcriptions`) when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set and Groq is not, or when `--whisper openai` is forced
- Writes the downloaded video, frames, audio, and an intermediate transcript to a working directory under the system temp dir (or `--out-dir` if specified) so Claude can `Read` them
- Reads / creates `~/.config/watch/.env` (mode `0600`) to store the Whisper API key(s) and a `SETUP_COMPLETE` marker. As a fallback, also reads `.env` in the current working directory

**What this skill does NOT do:**
- Does not upload the video itself to any API — only the extracted audio goes out, and only when native captions are missing AND Whisper is not disabled with `--no-whisper`
- Does not access any platform account (no login, no session cookies, no posting) — yt-dlp only ever requests public data
- Does not share API keys between providers (Groq key only goes to `api.groq.com`, OpenAI key only goes to `api.openai.com`)
- Does not log, cache, or write API keys to stdout, stderr, or output files
- Does not persist anything outside the working directory and `~/.config/watch/.env` — clean up the working directory when you're done (Step 5)

**Bundled scripts:** `scripts/watch.py` (entry point), `scripts/download.py` (yt-dlp wrapper), `scripts/frames.py` (ffmpeg frame extraction), `scripts/transcribe.py` (caption selection + Whisper orchestration), `scripts/whisper.py` (Groq / OpenAI clients), `scripts/setup.py` (preflight + installer)

Review scripts before first use to verify behavior.

cd /Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course && cp RESOURCES.md "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/RESOURCES.md.bak5" && python3 << 'PYEOF'
import io
p='RESOURCES.md'
s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a = "### One worked lesson thread: attentional focus"
assert a in s

v = """### ⭐ The single most useful source found so far — Gray's "3 Questions" video

**[A Call for More Clarity on How to Use the CLA: The 3 Questions Paper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0pLFDG-I78)** — Rob Gray, 17 Sep 2024, 47 min. Watched in full and transcribed 2026-09-02. His review of **Sports Coaching Review**'s "Adding texture to the art of constraints-led coaching: a request for more research-informed guidelines" ([doi:10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135)) — **same journal as the Yearby anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`).**

**Why it outranks everything else here: the paper asks the exact three questions Joe will ask, and Gray answers them operationally.** The critics demand rules for *which constraint, how much, how long*. Gray says a deterministic recipe is impossible in a complex system — **and then gives a usable decision procedure anyway.**

**1. The 70–75% success rule — the operational core, and the drill tool's default logic.**
> *"I let the 70, 75% rule be the guide… if they're achieving that kind of ideal range of success, that's the right challenge level."*

**Above ~75%: add complexity or a constraint. Below ~70%: reduce variability. Inside the band: leave it alone.** **This is the concrete answer to the challenge-point question that `RESOURCES.md` already names as the core problem the phase-2 tool must solve** (see the Harjiv Singh LinkedIn section). **Success rate is the trigger, not time, not rep count, not the clinician's eye.**
*Caveat to teach: it is Gray's practical heuristic from coaching experience, stated in a podcast — not a validated threshold. Treat it as a starting default the tool exposes and the user can change, never as a validated cut-point.*

**2. His actual iterative loop — write this straight into the tool:**
1. Pick the **invariant** you want, not the technique. His baseball example: the pitcher's back foot kept leaving the rubber. **He did not prescribe a foot position** — toe, heel, more knee bend were all fine. He wanted only *stay connected to the ground and transfer force.*
2. Add one constraint (he used a small ramp under the heel).
3. Give it **at least five or six trials** and watch: **is the movement solution changing at all?**
4. **Changing in the right direction → leave it in** until the new solution stabilises.
5. **Stabilised, or they cannot find a solution → manipulate it** (he varied ramp height).
6. **No effect at all → throw it out and design a different constraint.** *"I guarantee you will design a constraint that doesn't work at all. It happens to everyone, me included."*

**3. Variability scales to the individual's success — and this is exactly the regression/progression logic Joe needs.** Same session, same drill: the kid hitting every lay-up gets **more** variability (defenders, new angles, a deliberately bad pass to handle); the kid missing gets **less**. **That is a progression and regression rule derived purely from drill design, with no injury framing at all — the clearest demonstration in this file that good drill design and good return-to-performance dosing are the same skill.**

**4. He redefines "error", and it reframes what Joe should be watching.** In this approach the athlete never intends a *movement pattern* — they intend an *outcome*. So deviation from textbook form is not an error. His example: Steph Curry's off-balance one-handed three over two defenders in the Olympic final. **No coach would teach that shot. It went in. It was a solution that fit the constraints, not a mistake.** **Practical consequence for Joe: stop scoring the movement, score the outcome.**

**5. Where he concedes the clinician's ground — quote this to a physician.** Gray is explicit that ecological coaches do **not** just stand back: *"we're guiding self-organization, we're not just standing back and letting athletes do anything."* There are **invariant properties a solution must have**, and he names **a movement pattern that might cause injury** as a legitimate reason to step in. **This is the sentence that makes the whole approach defensible in a medical meeting**, and it pairs with Yearby's principle 5 on the Emergence blog, which says the same thing.

**6. Two arguments Joe will need, pre-made.**
- *"Constraints don't cause behaviour."* A constraint **interacts** with every other constraint, including the athlete's own. Anyone asking which constraint produces which outcome has misunderstood the causality. Expect the drill you designed to produce a different behaviour than you intended — **that is the system working, not a design failure.**
- *"These questions are not special to the CLA."* Nobody can say how long a traditional football passing drill should run, or how many reps. **The demand for precision is being made only of the new approach.**

**Football content is present**, unprompted: fewer defenders downfield affords the throw; a bigger gap affords the run; and he uses "how long should a passing drill be" as his worked example of the double standard.

**Use for:** the spine of the drill-design lessons, and **the specification for the phase-2 tool's core loop.** Cite as **expert practitioner commentary** — it is a podcast, not peer review — but he is the co-author of Joe's textbook and is reviewing a published paper, which puts it well above blog tier.
**Watch order for Joe:** this one first, then [Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gEMSjM1VS3c) (his most-viewed), then [How Effective are Coaches at Designing and Adapting Practice in the CLA?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xu39gkvGuVw).
**Also on the channel:** [an interview with Alex Sarama](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTXMVsSu1Q0) (ep 489) — the two threads of this file meet.

"""
s = s.replace(a, v + a, 1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print("RESOURCES.md updated —", len(s.splitlines()), "lines")

p='NOTES.md'
s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a = "## The tool (phase 2 — do not start until lessons land)"
assert a in s
s = s.replace(a, """## The tool — its core logic is now specified (2026-09-02)

**Do not re-derive this.** Rob Gray states an operational rule in [the 3 Questions video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0pLFDG-I78) (47 min, transcribed 2026-09-02; full notes in `RESOURCES.md`):

- **Success rate is the trigger — not reps, not minutes, not the clinician's eye.**
- **Above ~75% success → add a constraint or complexity. Below ~70% → reduce variability. Inside 70–75% → leave it alone.**
- Loop: choose the **invariant** (never the technique) → add one constraint → **watch 5–6+ trials** → changing in the right direction? leave it → stabilised or stuck? manipulate it → no effect at all? bin it and design another.
- **Same drill, opposite directions for different athletes**: the one succeeding gets more variability, the one failing gets less. **That is a progression/regression rule built purely from drill design — the proof that the design layer and the RTP dosing layer are one skill.**

**Treat 70–75% as an exposed, editable default in the tool, not a validated threshold** — it is Gray's practical heuristic from a podcast, not a study.

""" + a, 1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print("NOTES.md updated")
PYEOF
rm -rf "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/graywatch" && echo "work dir cleaned"

**[489 — Interview with Alex Sarama, Transforming Basketball](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTXMVsSu1Q0)** — 23 Apr 2024, 51 min. Transcribed in full.

**Read this before acting on the Sarama entry above.** Judged on his marketing site he looked like a source of drill examples. **In a 51-minute technical conversation with an academic he is substantially more than that, and one claim in this file was too strong.**

**CORRECTION to the entry above.** That entry says he has *"no rehab, injury or RTP content anywhere."* **True of his published output; false of his practice.** Describing three years at an Italian academy he says they went all in on the CLA *"not just on the court but in performance analysis, scouting, athletic performance, physical therapy"* — **he names physical therapy explicitly.** He has done this work across the medical seam; he simply has not written it up. **Do not tell Joe he has nothing to say here.**

**1. He independently reproduces Gray's success-rate rule — strong corroboration.** Tracking a player's finishing near the rim from practice video: *"he was averaging around 60%... it showed that what we're doing is the right level of challenge."* Then: *"I was watching stretches where he was getting eight out of ten and I just knew then I had to make it harder."* **Two practitioners, different sports, no coordination, same operating rule.** That materially raises confidence in the 70-75% default in the tool spec — **though it is still two expert opinions, not evidence.**

**2. "Rate limiters" — the missing input model for the phase-2 tool.** His central concept, and the most transferable idea in the interview. **Stop writing vague development goals.** He is blunt that *"become a better shooter, a better defender, pass the ball better"* means nothing. Instead diagnose the **specific** thing limiting **this** athlete.
His worked example is a masterclass and translates straight to football: a player was poor at rebounding. The standard fix was throwing the ball off the backboard 1-on-0. Watching game possessions he found **two precise rate limiters** — (a) the player **was not attuning to ball flight**, head still turned, about two seconds late to see it; (b) **positioning**, consistently ending up under the basket where no rebound is available. He then designed a live activity for exactly those, **and took a third limiter — creating space in contact — to the strength coach.**

content.text:
Watched it. Here's what it is and the one thing I got wrong.

## The video

**"489 – Interview with Alex Sarama, Transforming Basketball"**
Rob Gray's podcast · 23 Apr 2024 · 51 minutes · [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTXMVsSu1Q0)

Gray interviewing Sarama, the week Sarama's book came out. He was at the Trail Blazers' G League team then.

## I have to correct myself

I told you Sarama has **no rehab content anywhere**. That was based on his website. In this interview he says that in Italy he ran the CLA across **"performance analysis, scouting, athletic performance, physical therapy."**

**He has done this work with medical staff. He just never wrote it up.** I've flagged the correction in both places in the file.

## Two things worth taking

**1. "Rate limiters."** Stop writing vague goals. "Get better at rebounding" is useless. He watched game film and found two exact problems: the player **wasn't looking at the ball in flight** — head still turned, about two seconds late — and he **stood under the basket**, where no rebound ever lands. Then he built a drill for those two things, and took a third one to the strength coach.

**That is the missing input for your drill tool.** Position and injury are not enough. It has to ask what *specifically* limits this athlete, and push back if the answer is fuzzy.

**2. "Scripted start, live finish."** Script how the play begins. Leave the ending completely open. **That is how Joe gives an athlete twenty reps of one exact problem without deleting the reading part.** It is also the answer when medical staff ask about going live.

## A number I got wrong

I nearly wrote that Sarama backs up Gray's 70–75% rule. **He doesn't quite.**

- Gray: **70–75%** is the right difficulty.
- Sarama: **~60%** is already right.
- **Both** agree that around **80% means make it harder.**

They agree on *how* it works and disagree on *where* by 10–15 points. So the tool should ship a **slider showing both names**, not one number that looks proven.

## Where it lives

- `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md` — now 373 lines
- `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/NOTES.md` — tool spec updated

One caution I wrote into the file: both transcripts are **YouTube auto-captions**. They spell his name "Sama" and Myszka "Shan Mish." I fixed the names against real sources, but any quote should be checked against the audio before it goes in a lesson.

**The four goals of the CLA — his own framework, and a usable checklist for auditing any drill:**
1. **Destabilise the existing non-optimal movement solution.** **The starting question for every drill:** *"What can I add to practice that's going to make that current solution not effective?"*
2. **Encourage exploration and self-organisation.** Guide with an occasional suggestion; never prescribe.

**Definition worth putting in `GLOSSARY.md` verbatim:** a constraint is **"a feature of an individual, task or environment that takes away some of the movement solutions that can be used."** His analogy: a microwave has dozens of buttons and everyone uses two.
