Watched it. This one is the best of the three.

## The video

**"Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) 2024"**
Rob Gray · 22 Apr 2024 · **25 minutes** · his most-viewed, 4,649 views · [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gEMSjM1VS3c)

It is a preview of a talk he gave the **Netherlands Olympic team**. The other two videos defend the method. **This one just explains it.** Joe should watch this one first.

## The example you want

A pitcher's arm swings away from his body too early. Two problems at once:

- He **throws slower** — the power leaks out.
- He **strains the elbow ligament**. This is the injury that ends baseball careers.

The fix: put a **small rubber ball under his arm**. One instruction — *"throw so the ball falls out forwards."*

That is it. **Nobody ever mentions his arm.** And which way the ball drops tells him whether he is getting closer. Backwards means no. Forwards means yes.

**One injury. One constraint. No cue about the body part.** That is your whole course in a single example.

## The line for you specifically

Gray found the hitter's problem with **biomechanics** — his hips and shoulders weren't separating enough.

**He never told the athlete that.** Telling a hitter to rotate his hips makes him think about his hips, which wrecks the swing.

> "This biomechanics is for the coach to design constraints. That's the main thing it's for."

**Your force plates and GPS build the drill. They do not become the coaching cue.** I wrote that into the tool rules.

## And one that will sting a little

> "If the player is doing the worst ugly swing you've ever seen but their bat speed is high, **leave it alone.** Don't change things unless there's a good reason."

Only two good reasons exist: **performance or injury.** Not "it looks wrong." In a rehab room, "it looks wrong" starts a lot of interventions.

## One caution

He mentions studies saying CLA training **lowers ACL risk markers** and gets the **same skill in fewer reps**. If true, that second one is huge for you — same result, less wear on the athlete.

**But he names no papers, and the captions garble one title beyond recovery.** I wrote it into the file as a *things to go find* list, not as evidence. **Do not put those numbers in front of a doctor yet.**

## Where it lives

- `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md` — now 417 lines
- `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/NOTES.md` — new lesson-0001 candidate, plus the biomechanics rule
- Backup: `/Users/kristinarash/.claude/jobs/3ba15b10/tmp/RESOURCES.md.bak7`

You now have **four** candidates for lesson 0001. I labelled them as candidates rather than pretending one wins — that call belongs to the `/teach` session.

import io
p='RESOURCES.md'
s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a = '### ⭐ "Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) 2024"'
assert a in s

v = """### "How Effective are Coaches at Designing and Adapting Practice in the CLA?" — the only peer-reviewed evidence in this video set

**[Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xu39gkvGuVw)** — Rob Gray, 12 Aug 2025, 13 min. Transcribed in full 2026-09-02.
**Source note: quotes are from YouTube auto-captions, lightly cleaned.**

**Underlying paper (verified independently, 2026-09-02 — the captions garble every author name):**
**Goes, A. L., Machado, J. C., Bosco Júnior, J., Araújo, D., Leonardo, L., Bedo, B., & Scaglia, A. J. (2025).** The influence of coaches' intervention on the technical-tactical performance dynamics of young soccer players. SAGE. [doi:10.1177/17479541251348090](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17479541251348090) *(journal name not confirmed from an accessible source; the DOI is verified.)*
**Duarte Araújo is a co-author** — one of the founding names of ecological dynamics. **This is not a fringe paper. Strong candidate to add to Zotero.**

**1. Gray's four-step coaching cycle, from his new book — the process model the phase-2 tool should support.**
**Design** the constraint for this specific athlete or team → **put it in play and adapt** it from what you see → **guide** it with instructional constraints → **reflect and redesign.** **Note that "adapt" and "reflect" are steps, not afterthoughts. A tool that only helps with step one has done a quarter of the job.**

**2. The study design is unusually clean, and worth teaching as a model of asking a real question.** Three coaches (5–13 years' experience), 16 U-17 soccer players. Each coach designed a small-sided game for a tactical aim of their choosing, then ran it under **four conditions**: (1) **no intervention** — set it and walk away; (2) **verbal intervention only**; (3) **game intervention only** — change the pitch, players, rules, targets; (4) **free** — anything. Outcomes measured by notational analysis **plus positional variables**: possession duration, players involved, touches, **surface area covered, stretch index, centroid**.
**Those positional measures are computable from Baylor's own GPS data.** **If Joe ever wants to show a coach that a constraint changed behaviour, this paper is the template for how to measure it.**

**3. The headline finding, and it is uncomfortable for clinicians.**
- **Coach A (most experienced): none of the interventions improved anything.** The initial design was already working. Gray's gloss: *"in certain situations there's no need for intervention beyond the design."*
- **Coach B: verbal intervention did nothing. Changing the physical constraints did.** Significant changes in touches and possession only when the task itself changed.
- **Coach C (least experienced): both worked** — either because the original design was weaker, or because they read the session better. **The study cannot separate those two, and Gray says so.**

**In two of three coaches, talking to the players changed nothing measurable; changing the task did.** **This is the empirical version of the coaching-side claim already in this file — if you are constantly instructing, you have a design problem.** **Teach it to Joe early:** a clinician's reflex under pressure is to coach harder and talk more. **The evidence here says redesign the task instead.**

**4. "Pedagogical attunement to task dynamics" — the authors' term for the actual skill.** Reading what is happening in front of you and knowing **which lever to pull** — say something, change something, or deliberately do nothing. **Different coaches were good at different levers.** **Promote to `GLOSSARY.md` once Joe uses it correctly; it names the thing the whole course is trying to build.**

**5. "Sometimes the right intervention is none" — the hardest lesson for a clinician, and it has a citation.** Coach A's players performed best when left alone. **Good design buys the right to be quiet and watch.** For an athletic trainer whose professional instinct is constant vigilance and correction, this is the most challenging finding in the file — **and unlike most of what is here, it is peer-reviewed.**

**6. Why n-of-1 work matters, stated plainly.** *"There's no way you could do this at a group level... you'd lose all the information if you averaged across the three coaches."* Three coaches, three different effective strategies; the mean describes none of them. **This is the methodological justification for the single-case ACL study (`2MPW3ZQ3`) and for treating Joe's own athletes individually rather than by protocol.** Same theme as his channel video *Do Averaged, Group Data Accurately Capture Individual Movement Solutions?*

**Use for:** the four-step cycle as the tool's process spine; the "change the task, not your talking" lesson; the measurement template if Joe ever needs to prove a constraint worked; and the licence to leave a well-designed session alone.

"""
s = s.replace(a, v + a, 1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print("RESOURCES.md updated —", len(s.splitlines()), "lines")

p='NOTES.md'
s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a = "- Build toward the tool. Each lesson should surface one input the drill-design tool will"
assert a in s
s = s.replace(a, """- **Peer-reviewed lesson found 2026-09-02 — and it targets a clinician's reflex directly.** Goes,
  Machado, Bosco Junior, **Araujo**, Leonardo, Bedo & Scaglia (2025), [doi:10.1177/17479541251348090](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17479541251348090)
  ([Gray's review](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xu39gkvGuVw)). Three coaches ran the same small-sided
  game under four conditions: no intervention, verbal only, task change only, free. **In two of three
  coaches, verbal intervention changed nothing measurable. Changing the task did.** And the most
  experienced coach's players did best when **left completely alone** — the design was already right.
  **Joe's trained reflex under pressure is to coach harder and talk more. This says redesign the task,
  or say nothing. It is peer-reviewed, which most of this file is not.**
- **The tool must cover the whole cycle, not just step one.** Gray's four steps: **design → put in play
  and adapt → guide → reflect and redesign.** A tool that only proposes an initial drill has done a
  quarter of the job. **Adaptation is where the coaches in that study actually differed.**
- Build toward the tool. Each lesson should surface one input the drill-design tool will""", 1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print("NOTES.md updated")

I have to correct a number here. My grep said "football: 33 mentions." **That's misleading.** Most of those are the book title, section headings, and the rule that says *use football examples*.

**Everything else is baseball, basketball or soccer.** Every one needs translating before a position coach hears it.

And the biggest hole is still open: **nobody has written down what a corner, a guard, or a slot receiver has to perceive and solve.** You can't design a representative drill without that. **That probably has to be built from Baylor's own GPS and film. It is a course output, not a reading gap.**

The one book that would help most is **on your shelf, unscanned.**

I have never spoken to him. I don't know what he knows, what he's tried, or what he actually wants.

**But this is not a research problem.** `/teach` has a mission interview built for exactly this. **No amount of me reading fixes it. Only starting fixes it.**

Based on the search results, here's what I found about constraints-led approaches in American football practice design:

## Overview

An ecological approach to practice design in American football supports coaches in helping players to coordinate skilled movement behaviours in dynamic performance environments. Through the utilisation of a constraints-led methodology, coaches could design practice tasks to offer opportunities for players to interact with challenging performance problems that vary in complexity levels.

## Key Principles

Coaches are encouraged to become "learning environment designers" that promote or constrain athlete opportunities for action, thereby shaping the emergence of functional movement patterns. Athlete–environment interactions should focus on "representative learning design" to promote greater action fidelity and encourage athletes to "solve football problems that vary in complexity".

## Practice Design Application

Instead of forcing drills and technique repetitions, likely written far in advance (generalised for groups of athletes, not for specific individuals), softly assembled practice activities allow the coach-athlete system to manipulate constraints to challenge athletes to solve performance problems at that time. ## ⭐ Knowledge — American football specific, found 2026-09-02

**This section exists because the file's biggest weakness was that almost every worked example came from baseball, basketball or soccer, while the workspace rule is football-only.** These sources are football, they are free, and one of them is written by a course pillar.

### Football Beyond The Stats — the football example bank

**[footballbeyondthestats.wordpress.com](https://footballbeyondthestats.wordpress.com/)** — *"Breaking Down On-Field Movement of the Game's Best."* Written by **Shawn Myszka** since **2013**. **Free, public, and still active — latest post 15 Jan 2026.**

**What it is:** a weekly **"Play of the Week"** through the NFL season, each one a single real play broken down as **a movement problem the player had to solve** — explicitly through the player-environment relationship, the problem posed, and the information that shaped the solution that emerged. Plus an annual **"Mover of the Year"** and **"All-Movement Team."**
Categories: **Movement First Philosophy** (the theory posts), **Specific Player Evaluations**, **Sunday's Play of the Day**.
Recent subjects include **Myles Garrett, Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs, James Cook, Jameson Williams, Isaiah Williams**.

**Why this matters more than anything else added today:** it is **a decade-plus archive of football-specific worked examples, free, by one of the three textbook authors.** Every other source in this file needs translating out of its own sport before Joe can use it. **This one does not.**
**Use for:** the worked example in every lesson; showing Joe what "seeing the problem, not the technique" actually looks like on tape he already knows; and a repeatable weekly habit — one play, one problem, one constraint that could recreate it.
**Honest limit:** this is **example material, not a demand profile.** It shows how *individual elite players* solved *specific* problems. **It does not close gap 3** (what a corner versus a guard versus a slot receiver systematically has to perceive and solve). **It is raw material toward that, and the best available.**

### The published critique — football-specific, and better than the generic rebuttal already listed

- **Bobrownicki, R., Carson, H. J., MacPherson, A. C., et al. (2022).** Constraints of the constraints-led approach in American football and comments on Yearby et al. (2022). *Sports Coaching Review, 15*(1), 46–58. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579) · [Edinburgh Research Explorer](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/constraints-of-the-constraints-led-approach-in-american-football-/)
  **A direct, peer-reviewed rebuttal to this course's anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`), in this exact sport, in the same journal.** The authors (University of Edinburgh) accept the CLA is a useful tool but argue that **as a standalone approach it carries mechanistic and epistemological problems that block experimental comparison and limit its novelty and real-world applicability**, and that drawing on a **wider set of theoretical perspectives** serves practitioners better.
  **This supersedes Fransen (`CBJGJQX5`) as the rebuttal to teach.** Fransen argues against skill-acquisition specialists in general; **this argues against this specific paper, about this specific sport.** **Teach the anchor paper and this together, in the same lesson.** A practitioner who has only heard the case *for* folds the first time a physician or coordinator pushes back — and the pushback he meets will look like this one.

### Shawn Myszka — the credentials this file previously understated

Recorded because the practitioners section describes him only as "movement-skill acquisition with NFL players."
**Performance advisor and movement/skill-acquisition specialist to individual NFL players since 2008 — among the first in the United States to apply an ecological approach in American football.** **Over 145 professional football players, including 7 All-Pro selections and 14 Pro Bowl selections.** Pro Performance Director at **Explosive Edge Athletics** (Minneapolis); **co-director of education at Emergence**; advises **a dozen-plus NFL players a year**. # Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **DRAFT — written from Eric's spoken brief on 2026-09-01, not yet confirmed with Joe.**
> The "Why" and every "Success looks like" bullet is an inference, not something Joe or
> Eric said. Edit freely. Per the teach skill, a mission the learner did not shape will
> not steer him — confirm or rewrite this before lesson 0001.

## Why
Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own the last mile of
return to performance: the phase after a player is medically cleared but before he is
turned loose in team period — where he has to show he can actually do his job, at his
position, against the chaos of the real game. Joe wants to make that phase his niche:
to be the person who runs the sport-specific demonstration that proves an athlete can
meet the demands of his position. He wants a defensible, repeatable method for it, grounded in
ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA), and a niche that makes him
the person the medical and performance staff send athletes to for the final bridge.

## Success looks like
- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- Joe can defend a return-to-performance recommendation using the design of the exposure, not only a strength or hop-test number.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints
- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **In-season.** Sessions must fit in small windows. One tangible win per lesson.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos.
- **Tool must run locally** — no cloud services or servers without Baylor IT approval.
- **ASSUMPTION (unconfirmed):** Eric Rash commissions and steers this; Joe is the learner. See `NOTES.md`.

## Out of scope
- Early-stage rehabilitation, tissue healing timelines, and the criteria for medical clearance. This course starts *after* clearance.
- Motor-learning theory disputes (schema theory vs. ecological) beyond the minimum needed to defend a drill.
- Sports other than American football.
- Building a full athlete-management system. The deliverable is one focused drill-design tool.

# Mission interview — Eric and Joe

**Purpose:** confirm or rewrite `MISSION.md`, which is currently **DRAFT and entirely inferred
from Eric's spoken brief.** Every "Why" line and every "Success looks like" bullet in it is a guess.
**Until this conversation happens, the course is being built for a person nobody has asked.**

**Time:** 45 minutes. **Do not** try to cover everything — Part 1 and Part 2 are the ones that
matter; the rest can happen over a second coffee.

**One rule: ask, then shut up.** The failure mode here is Eric describing the course and Joe
agreeing. Joe agreeing is not information. **If Joe's answer to a question is a version of what
Eric already wrote, ask "what would make that wrong?" before moving on.**

**Take notes verbatim where you can.** Joe's own words about his job are worth more than a clean
paraphrase — the lessons get written in his language, not ours.

---

## Part 1 — Does Joe want this? (MUST. Ask first. Do not skip.)

**This is the question Eric is most likely to skip, and the one that decides whether anything else
is worth doing.** The whole project assumes Joe wants to own this niche. **Nobody has checked.**

1. **"What do you want to be known for here in three years?"**
   *Open, not leading. Do not say "return to performance" first — see if he does.*

2. **"When a player is medically cleared but obviously isn't right yet — whose problem is that
   here, currently?"**
   *Tests whether the gap this course targets is a gap Joe actually experiences.*

3. **"Is that a problem you want to own, or one you'd rather someone else owned?"**
   *The direct version. Ask it plainly.*

4. **"What's the last time that phase went badly, and what happened?"**
   *A real story beats an opinion. If he has no story, the mission may be Eric's, not Joe's.*

5. **"I wrote up why I think you'd want this. Can I read it to you, and you tell me where I'm
   wrong?"** — then read the **Why** section of `MISSION.md` out loud.
   *Ask for the disagreement explicitly. "Sounds right" is not a confirmation.*

> **If Joe is lukewarm here, stop and rethink the project before writing a single lesson.**
> A course built for someone who did not ask for it will not get used, however good it is.

---

## Part 2 — Where is he actually starting? (MUST)

6. **"What have you already read or heard about ecological dynamics or the constraints-led
   approach?"** *Sets the floor. If it's zero, lesson 0001 changes completely.*

7. **"Describe a drill you ran last week for someone in that final phase. Walk me through it."**
   *Gold. This is the before-picture, and it becomes the worked example in lesson 1.*

8. **"How did you decide when he was ready for the next step?"**
   *Listen for: a test number, a time-based protocol, a feel, or a physician's call.
   Whatever he says is the thing the course is trying to add to.*

9. **"What do you do when a drill is going too well? Too badly?"**
   *This is the success-rate question in his own language. Compare against the 70–75% / ~60%
   band in `NOTES.md` — does he already have an implicit rule?*

10. **"What's the part of your job you feel least confident defending to a coach?"**
    *Points straight at lesson 1. Teach into the discomfort.*

---

## Part 3 — The real constraints (MUST for lesson design)

11. **"Realistically, how much time per week — for learning, and for running these sessions?"**
    *`MISSION.md` assumes short in-season windows. Confirm the actual number.*

12. **"Where do you physically do this work? What equipment and space do you actually get?"**
    *A drill tool that suggests things he cannot set up is useless.*

13. **"Who has to say yes before you change how a session runs?"**
    *Names, roles. This determines who the arguments in `RESOURCES.md` are aimed at.*

14. **"Who's most likely to push back, and what will they say?"**
    *Pre-load the rebuttals. We have Bobrownicki (2022), the comparative-training material,
    and Gray's answers ready — but only if we know which objection is coming.*

15. **"Does anything you design have to end up in the medical record?"**
    *Answers open question 2 in `NOTES.md`. A record-producing tool needs Ath_Medicine review;
    a design aid does not. Currently assumed: design aid only.*

---

## Part 4 — What he already has (NICE, but high value)

16. **"Which positions do you see most in this phase?"**
    *Every lesson example gets written for those positions first.*

17. **"Which injuries?"** *ACL, hamstring, ankle, shoulder, concussion — the mix decides
    which library papers get used.*

18. **"Do you watch film? Can you get it?"**
    *If yes, Myszka's Football Beyond The Stats habit — one play a week, broken down as a
    movement problem — becomes a real practice, not a reading suggestion.*

19. **"What data can you actually see — GPS, force plate, anything?"**
    *Governed by the rule in `NOTES.md`: data informs the constraint, never the cue.*

---

## Part 5 — The tool (NICE — phase 2, but cheap to ask now)

20. **"If you had something that helped you design one of these sessions, what would you type
    into it?"** *Do not describe the tool first. Let him describe the input.*

21. **"And what would you want back?"** *A drill? A checklist? A reason to give a coach?*

22. **"Would you use it in front of a player, or the night before?"**
    *Decides whether this is a fast lookup or a planning surface.*

---

## Part 6 — Logistics (MUST — blocks the first session)

23. **"Do you want to do these sessions yourself at a keyboard, or do you want me to teach
    them to you?"**
    *This is open question 1 in `NOTES.md` and it changes the voice of every lesson.
    The `teach` skill assumes the learner is typing.*

24. **"How do you want to be pushed — told when you're wrong, or led to it?"**

25. **"What would make you quit this?"** *Ask it. The answer is usually time, and knowing that
    changes lesson length.*

---

## Immediately after the interview

1. **Rewrite `MISSION.md` in Joe's words and delete the DRAFT banner.** If the Why changed,
   that is a learning record per the teach skill.
2. **Answer the three open questions at the top of `NOTES.md`** — who drives, record-vs-aid,
   community participation.
3. **Pick lesson 0001 from the four candidates in `NOTES.md`** using what Joe said in Q7 and Q10.
   The candidates are: the agility/COD hook, the "1-on-0 deletes the task" hook, the attentional-
   focus chain, and Gray's connection-ball example. **Q10 should decide it.**
4. **Then start `/teach`.**

---

## Questions deliberately NOT on this list

- Anything asking Joe to evaluate the source material. He has not read it; that is the course's job.
- Anything about ecological-dynamics theory. Testing him on vocabulary before teaching it
  puts him on the back foot in the first conversation.
- "Does this sound useful?" **He will say yes. It tells you nothing.**

5. **"I wrote up why I think you'd want this. Can I read it to you, and you tell me where I'm
   wrong?"** — then read the **Why** section of `MISSION.md` out loud.
   *Ask for the disagreement explicitly. "Sounds right" is not a confirmation.*

> **If Joe is lukewarm here, stop and rethink the project before writing a single lesson.**
> A course built for someone who did not ask for it will not get used, however good it is.

---

## Part 2 — Where is he actually starting? (MUST)

6. **"What have you already read or heard about ecological dynamics or the constraints-led
   approach?"** *Sets the floor. If it's zero, lesson 0001 changes completely.*

7. **"Describe a drill you ran last week for someone in that final phase. Walk me through it."**
   *Gold. This is the before-picture, and it becomes the worked example in lesson 1.*

8. **"How did you decide when he was ready for the next step?"**
   *Listen for: a test number, a time-based protocol, a feel, or a physician's call.
   Whatever he says is the thing the course is trying to add to.*

9. **"What do you do when a drill is going too well? Too badly?"**
   *This is the success-rate question in his own language. Compare against the 70–75% / ~60%
   band in `NOTES.md` — does he already have an implicit rule?*

10. **"What's the part of your job you feel least confident defending to a coach?"**
    *Points straight at lesson 1. Teach into the discomfort.*

---

## Part 3 — The real constraints (MUST for lesson design)

11. **"Realistically, how much time per week — for learning, and for running these sessions?"**
    *`MISSION.md` assumes short in-season windows. Confirm the actual number.*

12. **"Where do you physically do this work? What equipment and space do you actually get?"**
    *A drill tool that suggests things he cannot set up is useless.*

13. **"Who has to say yes before you change how a session runs?"**
    *Names, roles. This determines who the arguments in `RESOURCES.md` are aimed at.*

14. **"Who's most likely to push back, and what will they say?"**
    *Pre-load the rebuttals. We have Bobrownicki (2022), the comparative-training material,
    and Gray's answers ready — but only if we know which objection is coming.*

15. **"Does anything you design have to end up in the medical record?"**
    *Answers open question 2 in `NOTES.md`. A record-producing tool needs Ath_Medicine review;
    a design aid does not. Currently assumed: design aid only.*

---

## Part 4 — What he already has (NICE, but high value)

16. **"Which positions do you see most in this phase?"**
    *Every lesson example gets written for those positions first.*

17. **"Which injuries?"** *ACL, hamstring, ankle, shoulder, concussion — the mix decides
    which library papers get used.*

18. **"Do you watch film? Can you get it?"**
    *If yes, Myszka's Football Beyond The Stats habit — one play a week, broken down as a
    movement problem — becomes a real practice, not a reading suggestion.*

19. **"What data can you actually see — GPS, force plate, anything?"**
    *Governed by the rule in `NOTES.md`: data informs the constraint, never the cue.*

---

## Part 5 — The tool (NICE — phase 2, but cheap to ask now)

20. **"If you had something that helped you design one of these sessions, what would you type
    into it?"** *Do not describe the tool first. Let him describe the input.*

21. **"And what would you want back?"** *A drill? A checklist? A reason to give a coach?*

22. **"Would you use it in front of a player, or the night before?"**
    *Decides whether this is a fast lookup or a planning surface.*

---

## Part 6 — Logistics (MUST — blocks the first session)

23. **"Do you want to do these sessions yourself at a keyboard, or do you want me to teach
    them to you?"**
    *This is open question 1 in `NOTES.md` and it changes the voice of every lesson.
    The `teach` skill assumes the learner is typing.*

24. **"How do you want to be pushed — told when you're wrong, or led to it?"**

25. **"What would make you quit this?"** *Ask it. The answer is usually time, and knowing that
    changes lesson length.*

---

## Immediately after the interview

1. **Rewrite `MISSION.md` in Joe's words and delete the DRAFT banner.** If the Why changed,
   that is a learning record per the teach skill.
2. **Answer the three open questions at the top of `NOTES.md`** — who drives, record-vs-aid,
   community participation.
3. **Pick lesson 0001 from the four candidates in `NOTES.md`** using what Joe said in Q7 and Q10.
   The candidates are: the agility/COD hook, the "1-on-0 deletes the task" hook, the attentional-
   focus chain, and Gray's connection-ball example. **Q10 should decide it.**
4. **Then start `/teach`.**

---

- Anything asking Joe to evaluate the source material. He has not read it; that is the course's job.
- Anything about ecological-dynamics theory. Testing him on vocabulary before teaching it
  puts him on the back foot in the first conversation.
- "Does this sound useful?" **He will say yes. It tells you nothing.**

That one I can't help with — stripping DRM means breaking a copy protection, and I won't write instructions for it even on a book you paid for.

Here's what actually gets you the content, roughly in order of how well it works.

## 1. Email Rob Gray and ask

**This is the best option and people forget it exists.**

He runs a podcast specifically to get research to practitioners. He sells courses to people exactly like you. You are a **Director of Applied Performance at a Power 4 school** building a staff course around his work.

Ask him for a PDF or EPUB. Independent authors say yes to that a lot. His email is in his YouTube video descriptions, and he is on X as **@Rob_Gray_ASU**.

If he says yes, you get a clean searchable file and none of this matters.

## 2. Highlight as you read, then export

`read.amazon.com/notebook` → pick the book → **Export notes**.

That is a normal Amazon feature for your own highlights. Hand me the file and `/ingest-book` takes it directly.

**Cost:** I only see what you marked. Entries get logged as "supported" rather than "proven." Still very usable.

## 3. Just tell me what's in it

Read a chapter. Tell me the argument in your own words. I write it up properly with citations and page numbers.

Slower, but honestly this often produces **better** course notes than raw text does, because you are already filtering for what Joe needs.

## What I'd do

**Send the email tonight.** It costs you two minutes, and Gray is unusually reachable. Highlight as you read in the meantime so you have something either way.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence (commit+push to KeystoneOS is standing-authorized per `feedback-auto-commit-push`; for any OTHER repo with changes, commit locally and list the push as an open item instead of pushing).

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- KeystoneOS: stage, commit with a descriptive message, push. Authorized.
- Other repos with changes: commit locally with a descriptive message; do NOT push without asking — list it in the final report instead.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Never push to a repo other than KeystoneOS without explicit approval.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.
